findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY — POST-EXTUBATION

Indication: Suspected myasthenic crisis; assess NMJ function post-acute event

TECHNIQUE: Low-rate (3 Hz) RNS performed at orbicularis oculi, nasalis, and abductor digiti minimi 72 hours post-extubation

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi (facial nerve): Decrement 18% from 1st to 4th stimulus [>10% = abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 15% ABNORMAL
  Abductor digiti minimi (ulnar nerve): Decrement 6% BORDERLINE NORMAL

FINDINGS: Significant abnormal decremental response in cranial nerve–innervated muscles (18%, 15%). Proximal and cranial NMJ dysfunction more pronounced than distal.

CONCLUSION: Electrophysiological findings indicate a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission with cranial-predominant pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Repetitive nerve stimulation: 18% CMAP decrement orbicularis oculi, 15% decrement nasalis (both above 10% threshold). Abductor digiti minimi 6% decrement (borderline normal). Cranial-predominant decremental pattern. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG REPORT — POST-EXTUBATION

Indication: Known AChR+ MG; confirm NMJ dysfunction severity post-crisis

TECHNIQUE: SFEMG of the extensor digitorum communis performed with voluntary activation

RESULTS:
  Mean consecutive difference (MCD): 68 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 28% of potential pairs showed intermittent blocking
  Fiber density: 2.1 (normal ≤2.0) MILDLY INCREASED

INTERPRETATION: Markedly increased jitter (MCD 68 µs; reference <35 µs) with 28% blocking rate. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

CONCLUSION: SFEMG confirms significant neuromuscular junction transmission failure. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION ANALYSIS — NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKING AGENTS IN MG

Query: Atracurium use in patient with myasthenia gravis

FINDINGS:
  ATRACURIUM (non-depolarizing NMB):
  - MG patients are MARKEDLY MORE SENSITIVE to non-depolarizing NMBs
  - Effect duration is prolonged and unpredictable in MG
  - Standard intubating doses may produce extended neuromuscular blockade lasting hours vs expected 30-45 minutes
  - Monitoring: Train-of-four (TOF) neuromuscular monitoring essential; do NOT use without TOF guidance
  - In acute crisis intubation: the benefit of airway protection outweighs risk; however, dose should be reduced by 50-75% if time permits
  - In this patient: Atracurium was administered at standard dose for emergency intubation — this will contribute to prolonged paralysis requiring ventilator support beyond resolution of acute crisis

  REVERSAL: Neostigmine can reverse atracurium; however, in MG patients neostigmine must be used with caution to avoid cholinergic toxicity on top of baseline cholinesterase inhibitor therapy

  SUCCINYLCHOLINE (depolarizing NMB):
  - MG patients may show RESISTANCE to succinylcholine (due to fewer functional AChRs)
  - Larger doses may be required; use cautiously

CONCLUSION: Atracurium use in myasthenia gravis is associated with markedly prolonged neuromuscular blockade duration. Train-of-four monitoring is recommended when non-depolarizing agents are used in this population. Clinical correlation recommended.
warnings: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents are markedly potentiated in myasthenia gravis; prolonged blockade duration should be anticipated; train-of-four monitoring is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT initiate aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone coverage for the aspiration pneumonia — substitute with piperacillin/tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole.
Do NOT extubate before objectively confirming adequate bulbar and respiratory recovery (cough, NIF, FVC).
required_recommendations: Empirical aspiration pneumonia coverage with NMJ-safe antibiotics
Hold pyridostigmine while intubated (per current practice) and resume as bulbar function recovers
Long-term plan: optimize immunosuppression (rituximab, eculizumab consideration) given recurrent crises

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: Myasthenic crisis (MGFA Class V), aspiration-precipitated, in patient with established AChR-positive MG post-thymectomy

differential.key_features: Aspiration is both the precipitant and a concurrent infection; CXR and ABG help characterize.
Patient on chronic pyridostigmine — check for muscarinic features; pyridostigmine hold may differentiate.
Aspiration plus respiratory failure raises sepsis concern.
Thymectomy 18 months ago; CT chest update reasonable but not the acute concern.
Always a differential in acute respiratory failure; selective imaging.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.

Myasthenic crisis = respiratory failure or imminent failure (FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP less negative than -30 cmH2O, weak cough, bulbar collapse) — ICU admission, urgent IVIG or PLEX, intubation criteria documented serially.
Recurrent crises despite thymectomy and pyridostigmine indicate refractory disease — escalate to long-term immunosuppression (rituximab, complement inhibitors).
Aspiration during swallowing studies in MG is a documented complication of bulbar weakness — protect the airway pre-emptively next time.

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST — INPATIENT

Clinical indication: Aspiration event during fluoroscopic swallowing study; respiratory failure

TECHNIQUE: Axial CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm slices, lung and mediastinal windows

FINDINGS:
LUNGS: Right upper lobe apical segmental atelectasis/consolidation, likely aspiration-related. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion. No other focal consolidation, masses, or ground-glass opacities.

MEDIASTINUM: Status post thymectomy — no visible thymic tissue. Small mediastinal lymph nodes measuring up to 7mm (not enlarged by CT criteria). Heart size normal.

PLEURA: No pleural thickening or effusion bilaterally.

DIAPHRAGM/UPPER ABDOMEN: Normal.

BONES: No acute bony abnormality.

IMPRESSION:
1. Right upper lobe apical segmental atelectasis consistent with aspiration event during swallowing study.
2. Post-thymectomy changes; no residual thymic mass or mediastinal adenopathy.
3. No additional pulmonary parenchymal disease, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion.

RECOMMENDATION: Follow-up chest imaging after extubation to confirm resolution of atelectasis.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 50-year-old South Asian man with a 2-year history of acetylcholine receptor antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis was admitted to the hospital for evaluation of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids over the past 3 months. He had undergone video-assisted thymectomy 18 months ago (pathology: thymic hyperplasia) and had experienced two prior episodes of respiratory decompensation requiring mechanical ventilation, both precipitated by upper respiratory infections. His baseline daily medications included pyridostigmine 60 mg every 6 hours, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and prednisolone 10 mg daily. At admission, he reported swallowing difficulty primarily with liquids causing coughing and choking spells, but no diplopia, ptosis, or limb weakness. Respiratory parameters on arrival were reassuring: NIF −42 cmH2O and FVC 2.8 L (82% predicted). He appeared alert and well-oriented with 5/5 limb strength bilaterally and intact gag reflex.

The gastroenterology team arranged an upper gastrointestinal fluoroscopic contrast study to characterize the degree of swallowing dysfunction. Under fluoroscopic guidance, approximately 8 mL of iohexol contrast agent was administered orally. Aspiration of contrast into the right main bronchus was immediately observed, and the study was aborted. The patient was transferred to the emergency unit on high-flow oxygen. Initial oxygen saturation was maintained above 92%, but over the ensuing 45 minutes his respiratory rate declined from 22 to 10 breaths per minute and he appeared paradoxically less distressed despite declining saturations to 87%. Nebulized salbutamol and a single intravenous dose of metronidazole 500 mg were administered without benefit. The clinical picture was attributed to aspiration pneumonitis, and the patient was intubated using IV midazolam and atracurium. Post-intubation chest radiograph showed right apical segment collapse. Upon ICU admission, the neurology team was consulted to reassess for possible neuromuscular contribution to the respiratory decompensation.
